prime.problem: A language model writes its answer one token at a time, and on a multi-step word problem the answer is often the very next token. One pass through the network has to do all the steps at once, and it often gets them wrong.
prime.fits: Builds on next-token prediction from the GPT build: the model only ever predicts the next token from what is already written. This card changes what gets written before the answer. Every later card in the course (voting, step grading, RL-trained thinking) starts from chains of thought.
expect: steps as a scratchpad later tokens attend to
prime.goal: Explain why writing steps before the answer helps a large model, why the paper's dots-only test rules out 'just more tokens', and when chain of thought is the wrong tool.

attend: What exactly differs between the standard prompt and the chain-of-thought prompt, given that the model is never retrained?
How does a partial result like the 3 in 23 − 20 = 3 reach the token that writes the final answer?
Which of the paper's ablations rules out 'extra tokens means extra compute' as the whole story?
Why does adding steps hurt a small model instead of doing nothing?
If a chain ends in the right answer, what does that tell you about the steps, and what does it not?

must: Few-shot examples show steps before 'The answer is' → the most likely continuation for the new question is steps too → the model writes its own chain with no retraining

Each token is one fixed-size pass → a direct answer must do every step in one pass → written steps split the work over many passes and leave each partial result in the text → later tokens attend to it
Dots instead of steps (6.4%) ≈ no steps (6.5%), and steps after the answer (6.1%) don't help → the gain needs informative steps written before the answer → real steps 14.3% (LaMDA 137B, GSM8K)
Each step must be within the model's reach → small models write fluent but illogical steps and errors carry to the answer → PaLM 8B 4.9% → 4.1%, PaLM 540B 17.9% → 56.9% on GSM8K
elevated: Gains are biggest on multi-step problems → one-step sums barely change (MAWPS SingleOp, PaLM 540B 94.1% both ways) → use it where there are steps to spread out
Nothing checks the steps → right answers can come from wrong steps (2 of 50 in the paper's hand check) → read a chain as text the model wrote, not a trace of its computation
reference: Eight hand-written exemplars for the maths sets (four for AQuA), greedy decoding, no fine-tuning
PaLM 540B with CoT (56.9%) beat fine-tuned GPT-3 175B with a verifier (55%) on GSM8K
Different annotators' exemplars all beat standard prompting (LaMDA 137B GSM8K: 15.5%, 17.6%, concise 11.1% vs 6.5%)
GSM8K = grade-school maths word problems (Cobbe et al. 2021)

compress.prompt: From memory, explain in 3–5 sentences why writing steps before the answer helps a large model and not a small one. Or redraw the token strip with the look-back arrows.
checklist: the examples in the prompt make steps the likely continuation; no weights change
one token = one pass, so a direct answer crams every step into one pass
written partial results stay in the text where later tokens attend to them
dots alone don't help, so the content of the steps matters, not just their number
a small model can't do each step reliably, so its chains are fluent but wrong

retrieve.q: Explain what a chain-of-thought prompt contains that a standard few-shot prompt doesn't, and how the model ends up writing steps for a question it has never seen.
answer: each example's answer includes the intermediate steps in words before 'The answer is'
the model copies the pattern of the examples
no training or fine-tuning is involved

retrieve.q: Walk through, token by token, how the model gets from 'The cafeteria had 23 apples' to writing 9, and say where each partial result lives.
answer: it writes 23 − 20 = 3, one token per pass
the 3 is now in the text
when writing 3 + 6 = 9, attention reads the earlier 3
the final answer token reads the written 9

retrieve.q: You serve a 7B model and want better maths answers. Argue whether to add chain-of-thought examples, and name the costs.
answer: at this scale the paper saw no gain or a loss
steps add output tokens: slower and pricier per answer
a bigger model or a trained reasoning model is the likelier fix
measure on your own problems before shipping

compare.q: Chain of thought writes one chain greedily; self-consistency samples many and votes. What does each fix, and how does each one fail?
answer: CoT gives the model room to work through steps
one greedy chain can still slip at any step
voting cancels scattered slips because wrong chains rarely agree
voting costs N times the tokens and fails when the model is wrong the same way every time

compare.q: This paper gets steps by showing examples in the prompt. R1-Zero gets long chains with no examples. What changed, and why does the newer approach not need the exemplars?
answer: CoT prompting changes the input, never the weights
R1-Zero trains the weights with RL, rewarding right final answers
the habit of writing long steps is learned because it earns reward
both rely on steps written before the answer

predict.q: Suppose you drop the eight worked examples and just add 'Let's think step by step' after the question (zero-shot). On GSM8K with PaLM 540B, where do you expect it to land relative to 17.9% (no steps) and 56.9% (eight worked examples)?
predict.answer: In between: 43.0%, as reported in the self-consistency paper (Table 8). The instruction alone gets the model writing steps, but the worked examples still teach a better format. Sampling 40 such chains and voting lifts it to 69.2%.

apply.task: Write one chain-of-thought exemplar for this problem: “A shop has 40 apples. It sells 15, then gets 3 boxes of 12. How many apples now?” Then write the standard (answer-only) version of the same exemplar, and mark which partial results a later token would need to look back at.
apply.done: Your exemplar has two written partial results (40 − 15 = 25 and 3 × 12 = 36), a final step 25 + 36 = 61, and ends with “The answer is 61.”; the standard version is just “The answer is 61.”
apply.hint: Match the paper's style: short plain sentences, each with one sum, before “The answer is”.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong before reading: did you expect the 8B model to improve?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why dots don't help, or why steps after the answer don't help?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: written partial result → attention reads it, or model size → each step within reach?
Where have you seen a chain of thought that sounded convincing but had a wrong step?
When would you pay the extra tokens for steps in a product you're building, and when not?
